rows.title: hlen  Device handlers that ignore the access length (audit)
rows.hold: census done; promote to a FIX round?

closure.note: Opened from the b75 refutation, then characterized by census. A device handler that switches on the address and cannot service a width will read or write only the first register of an 8-byte access. MEASURED SCOPE: 62 spanning-capable handlers of 167 registered; 20 on machines this project boots. TWO BOOTED MACHINES ARE PROVABLY IMMUNE - SH-4 has no 8-byte access at all (fmov.d is two 4-byte accesses) and MIPS32/R3000A treats LD/SD as reserved, so landisk and pmax cannot produce the access. NO CONVENTION EXISTS in the tree: no helper, no macro, no rule - only three hand-rolled decompositions that are all big-endian-specific and that disagree with each other about the else branch, so there is no single idiom to copy. FIRST WITNESS NAMED: dev_irqc on testarm, the only spanning-capable device on that machine, where the two halves of one aligned 8-byte access have OPPOSITE legal directions (status is read-only, mask is write-only), which makes the miss unambiguous. DETECTOR SHAPE: an offline differential in the diff_*.c family - no boot, no rig, no serialization.

entries.note: CENSUS: 118 files, 62 spanning-capable handlers, 20 on booted machines. Coverage PROVED by set-difference against the 167 registered handlers, not asserted. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS NOT WHETHER len IS MENTIONED: 115 of 167 pass len only to memory_readmax64, which marshals bytes and does nothing about a span across two registers - so 'uses len' does not mean safe, and the naive definition undercounts the class about 15 times. Also measured: fatal() DOES NOT HALT (debugmsg.c:384 is a plain wrapper), so the 8 warn-then-service handlers are the defect with a log line.

Apply complain-and-continue and a guest programming ordinary dual-address DMA gets NO BYTES MOVED, CHCR_TE never set, no interrupt -- it polls TE forever or reads a destination that was never written. Silent corruption or a silent hang surfacing in a driver far from the DMAC, strictly HARDER to diagnose than today's exit(1), which names the mode in one line.
* AND THE LATCH MAKES IT WORSE, NOT BETTER: for a hot STATUS register latching is right, but for a STATEFUL OPERATION the first dropped transfer reports and every later one is invisible -- the latch actively SUPPRESSES the evidence of accumulating divergence. That inverts the #433 refinement instead of extending it.
* Same class at sh4_pcic's window-base registers (PCIMBR :917, PCIIOBR :926, PCILAR0/1 :891/:909, PCILSR0/1 :882/:900): dropping a write leaves the emulator decoding at the OLD base while the guest believes it moved, so every later PCI access lands at the wrong address -- possibly on a different device that answers.

* THE ARM, stated so it applies per site: complain-and-continue is safe ONLY when the dropped write's only observable consequence is the register's own value. If the write's PURPOSE is to change how the emulator decodes, translates, transfers or invalidates -- address windows, TLB/cache flushes, DMA descriptors, coherency ops -- dropping it makes the model LIE rather than LAG, and the guest cannot tell. For that class: implement it, or stop honestly with cpu->running = 0 (which unlike exit(1) preserves the debugger and the emulator's own diagnostics) -- NEVER a latched drop. Three meanings, not two.
* AND THE ARM VINDICATES THE ROUND'S OWN SITE RATHER THAN BLOCKING IT: INT_ST_MASK IS state-changing (it is an SPL write), BUT the guarded portion -- bits 25..0 -- is MEASURED DEAD, so store-as-is drops nothing and the latched shape is correct at :816. rows.hold: REAL but optimisation-dependent; NOT the top item

entries.note: REPRODUCED TEST-FIRST, AND IT CORRECTS THE FILING AND MY OWN RANKING. MEASURED: SIGFPE with a core dump at -O0 and -O1, SURVIVES at -O2, -O3 and -Os, and SURVIVES under the tree's own build flags (-fgnu89-inline -O3 -DNDEBUG). At -O2+ gcc exploits the UB and elides the division. So the host does NOT die in the configuration this project builds. Still a defect -- UB on a guest-reachable path, restored by any debug build or compiler change -- but not the cheapest host kill and not top of the queue. THE optrow CLASS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE GLASS: optrow was a DETECTOR following the compiler, this is a DEFECT following it, and any severity claim about UB must name the flags it was measured under. The vacuity check mattered twice over: read-back confirmed dlab==1 and divisor==0 at the division with debug() reached, so the negative is not a skipped path; and the first run had ALL THREE probes dying INCLUDING THE CONTROL, because calloc left d->addrmult zero and the access function divides relative_addr by it -- the harness producing SIGFPE for the wrong reason, separated from the defect only by the control row.

CONFIRMED from source independently: the divisor is guest-zeroable via the DLAB low-byte write and the divide sits in argument position of a real varargs debug(), so it executes at every verbosity. Its follow-on hypothesis -- that this shape has other instances -- is now REFUTED by measurement: 24 diagnostic-argument divisions in src/, 22 with constant divisors, and the only other non-constant one (diskimage.c:543) cannot reach zero. rows.title: m8seg  A SEGMENT flush maps to ALL, and the over-invalidation is guest-visible
rows.hold: Behaviour change, not a records fix; the shipped direction is the SAFE one (under-invalidation is what leaves a stale translation). Filed from the R7 pass-2 grok seat, which attacked its own pass-1 advice.

entries.note: The fold sends CMMU_FLUSH_{USER,SUPER}_SEGMENT to the all=1 arm. Safe direction, but NOT free of guest-visible effect, and the shipped comment claimed it was. A walk writes PG_U (and PG_M on a write) back into the page descriptor IN EMULATED MEMORY; a PATC hit sets those bits only in the PATC copy. So a guest that clears U on a page in segment B, flushes segment A, then touches B observes a U bit a correctly-scoped flush would have left clear. The tighter mapping needs no manual: match the walker's own 4 MB segment size, (sar ^ vaddr) & 0xffc00000. What real silicon does at segment granularity is UNKNOWN -- there is no 88200/88204 manual in this project.

entries.note: SAR's whole justification for not purging is that its ONLY consumer is the SCR flush command, and that arm purges itself. NO ROW ANYWHERE COMPOSES THE TWO. diff_m8invread.c writes SAR and checks purge counts; diff_m8820x.c checks flush scope but SEEDS SAR DIRECTLY into reg[] rather than through the handler, so it structurally cannot see this arm. Wanted: write SAR through MMIO, assert no purge and unchanged PATC; then issue a PAGE flush and assert exactly one dyntrans purge with the MATCHING PATC entry removed and a non-matching entry RETAINED -- and the same sequence on cmmu_nr 1 and from a non-owner CPU. That is the row that would prove the justification rather than assert it.

rows.title: reprowitness  The reproducibility rule asks 'can this MACHINE boot' when it should ask 'can this CODE PATH be executed'

entries.note: RAISED UNPROMPTED BY THE MEASURE SEAT WHEN ASKED WHETHER THE RULE IS TOO HARSH, and it is the most consequential thing on this brief. The standing rule -- no reproduction means DOCUMENT, not fix -- is right, but it is being applied at MACHINE granularity. armbdt is the proof: there is NO bootable ARM rig here, yet gate 14 already scores 261 checks on `testarm` through the cold debugger with a four-byte raw file. Machine-boot granularity would have DEMOTED THE BEST ITEM ON THE LIST. Proposed restatement: *reproducible = an executable witness exists*, with probe witnesses ranked equal to boots. IT LAUNDERS NOTHING -- dfreq still ranks last under it, because it has no witness of either kind. THIS DIRECTLY REOPENS THE exitsweep SCOPE QUESTION, which was settled on rig availability: sites in devices no rig boots may still have probe witnesses.  [panel_20260817_174701]
